questions.q: What real failure mode does a `unique` test on dim_subscribers.subscriber_id catch?
options: An incorrectly formatted date
A slow-running dbt model
A missing column in the raw source table
Duplicate subscriber rows silently inflating Power BI's subscriber count
questions.explain: A dimension table with duplicate keys silently inflates any downstream count built on it -- the specific, damaging failure this test is designed to catch.

questions.q: How does dbt decide whether a singular test has failed?
options: The test is a SQL query; if it returns any rows at all, dbt considers it failed
dbt runs a separate validation engine unrelated to SQL
Singular tests always pass unless manually marked as failed
A singular test fails only if it throws a SQL error
questions.explain: A singular test's query is expected to return zero rows when everything is correct -- any returned row represents a case violating the rule being tested.

questions.q: What business rule does the assert_no_cancellation_before_signup singular test encode?
options: A subscriber's cancellation timestamp can never be earlier than their first-seen timestamp
Every subscriber must eventually cancel
Subscribers can only cancel on the same day they signed up
A subscriber cannot have more than one billing event per day
questions.explain: This is a Driftwood-specific business rule no generic test (not_null, unique, accepted_values) could express -- exactly the kind of thing a singular test is for.

questions.q: What does the accepted_values test on stg_billing_events.event_type actually guard against?
options: Incorrect data types on the amount_usd column
Duplicate subscriber_id values
Missing rows in the source table
A typo'd or unexpected new event type the pipeline wasn't built to handle, such as a new event type shipped without the data team being told
questions.explain: accepted_values catches values outside an explicitly defined expected set -- exactly the scenario of an unannounced new event type appearing in the data.

questions.q: What does the grain note on fct_subscriptions ("one row per event, not per subscriber") prevent, according to this lesson?
options: A Snowflake storage cost increase
A new analyst guessing the wrong grain and silently miscounting subscribers in a report
A dbt compilation error
A failed CI/CD pipeline run
questions.explain: Undocumented grain is a classic, silent source of wrong numbers -- someone building a report against the wrong assumed grain won't get an error, just a wrong result.
